body: Choosing can feel like a test with one right answer hidden somewhere. For the next ninety days, one line a day will help you practise deciding with less dread and more trust in yourself.
No need to change anything yet. Today, simply count how many small decisions you put off or handed to someone else.
Dithering is rarely laziness. Usually it is a way of avoiding the discomfort of possibly being wrong.
Notice the kinds of decisions that stall you. Big ones, tiny ones, ones involving other people, ones involving money?
When you get stuck, what does your mind say? Perhaps "I need more information", or "What if I regret it?" Just observe the line it uses.
See how long you spend on something low-stakes, like picking from a menu or choosing a film. Time it, out of curiosity.
Research can feel like progress. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is a comfortable way of not choosing.
Notice who you ask for opinions, and whether you are looking for advice or for permission.
Not deciding is also a decision. It just tends to be made by default, by a deadline or by someone else.
Think of a decision you made quickly that turned out fine. Let it stand as evidence that you can.
Notice what happens in your body as a choice approaches: tight shoulders, a churning stomach, a sudden urge to tidy.
Most choices are reversible, or at least adjustable. Count how many of the ones in front of you are truly permanent.
Write down the pending decisions taking up room in your head right now, so they stop circling.
Being decisive is not the same as being rash. It means giving a choice the attention it deserves, and no more.
Two weeks of watching. Which decision on your list would bring the most relief if it were simply made?
First experiment: for anything costing less than a coffee, decide within thirty seconds today. Notice that the world carries on.
Set a deadline for one stuck decision. Write the date down and tell someone, so it carries some weight.
When choosing between two similar options, flip a coin. Notice whether you feel relief or disappointment as it lands. That feeling is your answer.
Today, when someone asks where you would like to eat or what to watch, give a real answer instead of "I don't mind".
Try limiting your research: three reviews, or twenty minutes, then choose from what you know.
Ask of a stuck choice: what would I pick if I had to pick right now? Write the answer down, even if you do not act on it yet.
Good enough is a real standard. Pick one choice today and aim for good enough rather than perfect.
Settle one thing before lunch that you would normally leave until tomorrow.
When torn, ask which option you would rather explain to a friend in a year's time. Your reasons often clarify in someone else's company.
Make a small decision today and do not revisit it. No second-guessing, no checking the alternatives afterwards.
Experiment with fewer options. If you are choosing between eight, cut it to three first, then choose.
Ask how a choice will feel in ten minutes, ten months and ten years. Many worries shrink quickly under that light.
Notice one decision you have been making for someone else's approval. What would you choose if nobody would ever know?
Write the worst realistic outcome of a choice you are avoiding, then what you would do if it happened. Fear often shrinks on paper.
Make a choice and say it aloud in a plain sentence: I have decided to... Notice how it sounds in your own voice.
Pick a default for something recurring, such as a weekday breakfast or a Friday plan, so it no longer needs deciding.
A month in. Which experiment made deciding feel lighter? Use it again this week on something a little bigger.
When you catch yourself opening another tab of research, pause and ask what single question you are actually trying to answer.
Treat one choice as a trial rather than a commitment: I will try this for two weeks and see.
Ask yourself what you already know but are hoping someone will tell you is fine. Then trust it.
If others are waiting on you, decide one thing today that unblocks them. Being decisive can be a kindness.
Notice the hidden cost of something undecided: the evenings it fills, the low hum of worry. Is that cost worth the extra time?
Let a small decision be slightly wrong on purpose today, and watch how easily you adjust.
Name what matters most to you before a choice. Once you know that, the options often sort themselves faster.
Make choices when you are rested and fed rather than late at night. Timing can matter more than more information.
Practise saying "I haven't decided yet, but I will by Thursday." A decision about when to decide still counts as movement.
If you have asked three people, stop asking. Sit quietly with what you have heard and choose for yourself.
Watch how decisive people around you handle mistakes. Usually they just correct course without much fuss.
Try deciding things in the order they arrive today, rather than letting them pile up for later.
Choose one thing you have been meaning to buy, book or reply to, and do it before the day ends.
Look back over the experiments so far. Notice which ones you have quietly kept doing without being reminded.
Regret is real, but people tend to regret what they never tried more than the choices that did not work out. Let that steady you.
Start a decision log: one line on what you chose and why. Later, it will show you how often you were fine.
When perfectionism insists there must be a best option, remember that several options are often good in different ways.
If you feel the urge to reopen a settled decision, ask whether anything has actually changed, or whether it is just nerves.
Today, choose without announcing that you might be wrong. Skip the caveats and see how it feels.
Notice how much energy returns once something has finally been decided. Let that feeling become familiar.
Give yourself a worry budget: fifteen minutes to think it through, then a choice, then on with the day.
Some decisions are hard because both options involve loss. Being decisive means accepting that loss rather than waiting for it to vanish.
Make one choice today that is entirely yours to make, without consulting anyone. Notice any unease and let it pass.
When you hear yourself say "I'll think about it", add when. Thinking without an end point tends to turn into waiting.
Small decisions build the muscle for big ones. Every quick, settled choice is practice.
If you have stalled lately, pick the smallest pending choice and make it now. Momentum often starts tiny.
Listen to how you describe yourself. If you still say you are indecisive, try "I am learning to decide" instead.
You are nearly two months in. Before tomorrow's look back, recall one recent choice you are glad you made.
Time to take stock. Which experiments genuinely helped you decide, and which just felt like more rules? Keep the useful ones and drop the rest.
Pick the two tools that worked best for you and use them on purpose this week, rather than waiting until you are stuck.
You will still have days when you circle a choice for hours. That does not erase your progress. Notice it, then choose.
If a decision turns out badly, separate the outcome from the choice. You can decide well with what you knew and still be unlucky.
Take on a bigger decision now, one you have been carrying for a while. Use your deadline, your research limit and your plain sentence.
Notice whether others respond differently as you decide more readily. People often find clear answers restful.
When the old fear returns, it may be louder than usual, as if testing you. Thank it for trying to protect you, and choose anyway.
Read back through your decision log, if you kept one. Count how many choices turned out fine or better.
Deciding for yourself will sometimes disappoint someone else. You can be kind about their feelings without handing them the decision.
If a choice did not work, practise changing course without a long inquest. Adjust and move on.
Make one decision with incomplete information on purpose. Most real choices are made that way.
Notice where you still hand decisions to others to avoid blame. Take one of them back this week.
Some days tiredness will make every choice feel heavy. On those days, lean on your defaults and save the bigger ones for later.
Ask what you would advise a friend in your position. Then give yourself the same plain advice.
Notice the quiet confidence that comes from following through. A decision acted on teaches you more than one perfectly weighed.
If you slid back into endless research this week, do not scold yourself. Set a new limit and begin again.
In a meeting or group, offer a clear suggestion rather than taking the question away to think. See what happens.
Being decisive includes deciding not to do something. Close one option firmly today and enjoy the space it leaves.
Notice how much lighter your mental list is than when you began. Fewer open loops, more room to think.
When a choice feels huge, look only at the next small decision inside it. You rarely have to settle everything at once.
Remember a decision from these weeks that scared you. How does it look now that it is behind you?
Setbacks are part of this. One week of dithering does not mean you are back at the start.
Trust your first sensible instinct on a small matter today, without checking it against anything else.
Notice that being wrong now and then has not been the disaster your fear predicted. Let that sink in.
Make one decision this week that your future self will thank you for, even if it is uncomfortable today.
Think about who you are becoming: someone who weighs things fairly and then chooses. Notice where that is already true.
Write down the handful of habits that help you decide: perhaps deadlines, fewer options, a coin, a plain sentence. Keep the list somewhere handy.
You will not always feel certain. Decisive people rarely do. They simply choose without waiting for certainty to arrive.
Set yourself a gentle rule for the months ahead, such as deciding small things on the spot and big things by a set date.
When doubt returns, look back at the choices you have made over these weeks. You have plenty of evidence now.
Notice how much time and attention has come back to you since you started deciding sooner.
That brings these ninety days to a close. Keep choosing, keep adjusting, and trust that you can handle whatever follows from your decisions.
